newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 23.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SAINSBURY TO STOCK MORTGAGES

Supermarket group J Sainsbury is to offer mortgages in its stores after announcing a tie-up with Standard Life, Europe's largest mutual insurance company. The move follows Sainsbury's successful launch of banking services earlier this year, and comes on the day that rival chain Tesco launches a low-cost credit card.
-- SMITHKLINE DEAL WITH BAYER IN US

British pharmaceutical and healthcare group SmithKline Beecham SBa.L has secured US marketing rights for the latest in the fast-growing class of cholesterol-lowering agents known as statins. News of the deal to co-promote the product, which was developed by Bayer and is called Baycol, came as SmithKline reported a 16 per cent increase in second-quarter pre-tax profits to 398m stg.
-- FURNISHING GROUP HIT BY MERGER COSTS

Retail furnishings group H&C Furnishings has reported a 60 per cent plunge in pre-tax profits in the year to April to 905,000 stg, following the write-off of 7.8m stg in reorganisation costs from its 1996 merger with Harveys Holdings and Cantors. Group chairman Sir Henry Solomon stated results in the first ten weeks of the year were impressive, but attributed them to building society windfall spending. Cantors reported pre- tax profits of 2.19m stg in 1996 on operating profits of 7.9m stg. The H&C Furnishings results include nine months from Harvey.
THE TIMES
-- BAT PAYS 1BN STG FOR HALF OF MEXICO'S TOBACCO TRADE

Shares in BAT Industries rose 13.5p to 517.5p on Tuesday following the announcement that the tobacco-to-financial services group is to acquire Mexico's biggest cigarette maker for $1.7bn (1.01bn stg). Mexico is the last Latin American country in which BAT is not represented, and the deal will give it 50 per cent of the Mexican cigarette market.
-- BOEING RAISES HOPES ON EU BAN

US aerospace giant Boeing has offered further concessions to the European Commission in a last-gasp bid to prevent a European block on its proposed $14bn (8.35m stg) merger with McDonnell Douglas. The Commission is due to give its verdict on the merger on Wednesday, and, following the breakdown of talks last week is expected to reject it unless Boeing offers substantial new concessions.
-- ARNAULT RAISES GRANDMET STAKE

Bernard Arnault has moved to increase the stake his LVMH groups owns in Grand Metropolitan to almost 10 per cent. The move follows the rejection by GrandMet and its prospective merger partner, Guinness, of plans by Arnault for a three-way alliance involving the drinks businesses of the three groups. According to sources, LVMH, which opposes the Guinness/GrandMet merger, could have taken its stake in GrandMet to over 10 per cent, and reduced its holding in Guinness from 14.2 per cent to below 12 per cent.
THE GUARDIAN
-- INSURER PICKS UP HAMBROS TAB

It has been revealed that the aborted takeover by Hambros Bank of the Co-Operative wholesale society will not cost the bank any charges, as the tab has been covered by the group's insurer under its indemnity insurance policy. The announcement was made at Hambros' annual shareholder meeting which attracted a record attendance, as it marked the departure of Bank chairman Lord Hambros.
-- CBI BACKS SINGLE CURRENCY

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) has urged the government to agree in principle to join a European single currency. However, the group, which represents Britain's business leaders, also called on ministers to defer joining until after the scheduled start date of January 1 1999. The new approach, which echoes the government's own position, has been seen as further evidence of a rift between business and the Conservative party.
-- ITV LICENCE CHANGES WILL EASE CASH BLIGHT

The Independent Television Commission has called for a radical shake-up of the ITV licence system in an attempt to ease the burdens stemming from Margaret Thatcher's 1990 Broadcasting Act. It is expected the ITC will announce proposals on Wednesday which involve reducing the amount the companies contribute to the Treasury beginning in 1999 and protection of spending on programmes due to the competition brought on by satellite and cable programmers.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- PROFITS UP BY 176 PER CENT AT STAGECOACH

Rail and bus group Stagecoach has reported a 176 per cent rise in profits from 43.6m stg to 120.5m stg, due in large part to the number of acquisitions announced by the group in the last year. Stagecoach has also announced the resignation of Sandy Anderson just one year after making a 36m stg profit on the sale of the Porterbrook leasing company.
-- LITTLEWOODS CHIEF HAS 'FULL BACKING OF MOORES'

The chairman of Littlewoods, the privately-owned retail-to-pools group, has defended his decision not to sell the company's 135-store high street chain. James Ross was meeting shareholders from the Moores family, which owns Littlewoods, and who later issued a statement expressing their 'complete confidence in the chairman and the board'. Ross also reported a 6 per cent fall in annual profits.
-- BRITISH GAS IN NEW ROW WITH REGULATOR

British Gas has begun another dispute with gas industry regulator Clare Spottiswoode, claiming she has ignored a report by the Monopolies Commission into its TransCo pipeline by making proposals to cap the revenues it could earn. A BG spokesman stated as a result of the Ofgas director general's move, which it claims ignores the concept of incentive regulation, the company's financial outlook has been altered in a 'fundamental' way.
